utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone after a long time, in which we have not seen each other. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger or Mr. Waespi, I don't know who to address. Are you ready to -- is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Mr. Erik Lennart Widen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. No protective measures, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I already raise the issue now that from written submissions from the 13th, the 15th, and the 18th of August, it appears that the Defence has no objection against the admission of the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Widen. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you. Could you please make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Widen. Please be seated. Mr. Widen, you are not a native English-speaking person. If there would ever be any problem either in understanding or in expressing yourself in the English language, which I assume is the language in which you'll be examined and in which you will answer, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Gustafson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Widen, can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Widen, Erik Lennart.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown 65 ter number 5360, and if he could be provided hard copies of his witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Widen, do you recognise the statement you see on the screen and the first one of the two that were just handed to you as a statement you made and signed on the 14th of December, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And could the witness now be shown 65 ter number 5361, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Widen, do you recognise the statement on the screen now and the second one of the two that were just handed to you as a statement you made and signed on 26th and 27th of February, 2008, and in which you made a number of corrections and clarifications to your earlier 1995 statement?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we please move to page 5 of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 5 in paragraph 30, there's a reference there to the policija station referenced in paragraph 15 above. Should that in fact be a reference to paragraph 29 above?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And can we move to the appendix page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In paragraph 34 of this page, the first sentence says: "The looting in Knin went on for ten days from about 6 August to 16th August." And is that 10-day period, is that an exact period of time or an approximate period of time?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I would say approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And with those corrections to these two statements taken together, are they true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do the statements reflect what you said at the time they were taken?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if I asked you in court today the same questions you were asked when you gave these statements, would you give the Court the same answers that are in those statements?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender these statements into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, I take it also not after the small correction just made by the witness, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 05360 becomes Exhibit number P721; and 65 ter 05361 becomes Exhibit number P722.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P721 and P722 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I would like also to distribute to the Court and to each of the Defence teams hard copies of the photograph of Knin that's attached to the witness's second statement. The markings are hard to make out in e-court, and if I could read a summary of the witness's 92 ter statement at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that you have explained what the purpose of this is?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Erik Lennart Widen worked as an UNCIVPOL monitor in Knin between the end of June 1995 and approximately the 20th of August, 1995. On the 4th of August, he was woken by the sound of shelling at 5.00 a.m.. He took refuge in a corridor of his apartment where he stayed until approximately 6.00 p.m. the following day, when he took shelter in a neighbour's apartment. Mr. Widen observed that the shelling ceased at approximately 1.00 p.m. on the 5th of August. At approximately 3.00 p.m., he began hearing tanks and small-arms fire and could hear soldiers shooting and breaking down doors. At approximately 7.00 on the morning of 6 August, Mr. Widen left his neighbour's apartment and walked to the UN compound in Knin. A few hours later, he went on a foot patrol of Knin with another UNCIVPOL official. They saw soldiers driving military vehicles out of Knin that contained television sets and furniture and saw members of the Puma Brigade carrying goods that appeared to be stolen. Mr. Widen saw signs of shelling damage to several residential buildings in Knin. Mr. Widen observed that the looting of Knin continued for approximately ten days, beginning on the 6th of August. A check-point had been set up on the bridge over the River Krka in Knin by 7.00 a.m. on the 6th of August. The soldiers and police manning the check-point did not stop the vehicles filled with goods that soldiers were driving out of Knin. That completes the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Widen, I'd like to ask you a few questions about what's in your statements. I will begin by asking you one or two questions about events in Knin prior to the 4th of August; Most of my question also be about events in Knin on the 5th and 6th of August, and I will ask a few questions at the end about events after the 6th of August. My first question is about the mobilisation in Knin that you talk about at paragraph 43 of your 2008 statement. You described seeing a regiment of approximately 500 ARSK troops in Knin during a mobilisation that took place; And I'd like that ask you, how long before Operation Storm did this mobilisation take place, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No, I can't remember, but -- no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of what the extent of the presence of ARSK troops was right before Operation Storm, in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: After Operation Storm, you saw no Serbian soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right before Operation Storm, do you remember what the presence of ARSK troops was? Like, on the 2nd and 3rd of August.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: What I saw was those who were sitting in the cafes in Knin. There seems to be, let's say, not real soldiers but they were armed, and then outside the school, I mentioned in my witness -- I saw about 500 soldiers, and among them, also, this man Mladic. He was also there. And how many days, now, it is very difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you saying that you don't remember exactly how many days this was before Storm?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 50 of your 2008 statement, you describe how you heard the noises of vehicles leaving Knin on the night of the 4th, after the shelling had started, and you estimated that you thought about 80 per cent of the population left Knin on the night of the 4th and during the 5th. And I'd like to ask you: In the two or three days before Operation Storm, did you see any organised movement of civilians out of Knin?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you see any significant numbers of civilians leaving Knin before Operation Storm in those two or three days?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, one of the previous answers seems to create a problem. Your question was the presence of ARSK troops. The witness first answered by telling us what was the situation after Operation Storm. Then you repeated your question, said, what, like, on the 2nd and 3rd of August. Then the witness gave an answer, and then at the end he said, And how many days, it is difficult to say. So I would like to know that the 500 people you were asking about, was that at the moment you do not remember, or do you say it was two or three days before Operation Storm, but I do not know whether it was the 2nd or the 3rd; or was it longer ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's say, between -- it could be ten days before. It could be three days before. I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you're talking about the 500, you say it could be as many as ten days, but it could have been also two days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to events on the 5th and 6th of August. In your 1995 statement at the second page, which is marked as page 1, and as well, in paragraph 12 of your 2008 statement, you described how the shelling stopped about 1.00 p.m. and that you began to hear the sounds of tanks and small-arms fire at about 3.00 p.m. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber the sounds of small-arms fire that you heard?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: When I heard the fire from the small arms, it was down where I lived. It was a house with many apartments, and I heard the kick in the doors, and immediately after they kicked the door, I could hear machine-gun. So that's the time when I recognised that Croatian soldier have come into Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said you heard the kick of the doors, and immediately after the kick you heard the machine-gun fire. Do you remember approximately how many times you heard that pattern?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: It went out for hours, so ... how many times I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And where were you -- you were in your apartment at this time, according to your statement. Where exactly in your apartment were you?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I was sitting on the floor near the chimney because if the grenade have come, I thought that was the best place to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mm-hm. And when you heard the sounds of small-arms fire, did you hear anything to you that sounded to you like people were firing at each other or anything like an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your 1995 statement on the second page, you describe how you moved to the basement of your neighbour's apartment during the evening of the 5th of August, and you describe how there were about 15 other people in that basement and you say there were women, children, and some men. Do you remember approximately how many of the 15 or so people there were men?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I can't remember that, but less than half of the people there. Four, five men, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what was the atmosphere like in the basement with the other 15 people? How were the people feeling?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: They were scared, and they asked for my protection, and I said I do whatever I can, so I stay with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at the second and third pages of your 1995 statement and at paragraphs 15 to 20 of your 2008 statement, you describe how you left the flat where you were sitting with the other people at 7.00 a.m. in the morning of the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then you walked to the UN headquarters in Knin, and you passed a check-point manned by HV soldiers on the way.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you describe seeing soldiers during this walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have to object to that. The -- what he describes is a check-point that was manned by the military police and civilian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I think at paragraph 47 the witness states that when he first passed the check-point it was manned by HV soldiers in flat olive green fatigues, and then when he returned to the check-point later that day it was manned by military police and civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My read of that was that he was talking about the same set of people at the check-point, that these were the people there going in, these were the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that, of course, now becomes a matter which is -- the objection is denied, and I think it would have been a matter to seek clarification in cross-examination rather than to start debating the interpretation of what the statement actually said because the language as quoted by Ms. Gustafson seems to be correct one, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, then I would object to the leading at that point because, I mean, I've let the leading go so we could get through this expeditiously, but that was a clearly leading question, so it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge, but I just want to put on the record that if I can't, you know, interject when I think there's something in error, then I would object to the leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't consider it leading to refer to a witness's statement that's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was wondering; therefore I was re-reading. Yes. As a matter of fact, it might have been a superfluous question because it just repeats what is already in evidence. Mr. Kehoe, would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I actually -- I haven't gotten to my question yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, sometimes what is superfluous can be a way of introducing a next question. I'm aware of that, but I tried to get out of whether you misrepresented the statement of the witness, whether it was a leading question, or whether it was just putting to the witness what was already in evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Widen, I would like to ask you at this time, when you were walking to the UN compound you describe seeing soldiers and you state in your statement the soldiers were shooting all the time; whether for amusement or to frighten people, I can't say. And I would like you just to describe to the Trial Chamber the shooting that you observed when you were walking to the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: It was on the right side of the street. It was a lot of houses, small houses, and outside those houses the Croatian soldier were sitting, and they were drunk, celebration, perhaps, that they have come to Knin. I don't know. But they start shooting when I walk, and I have the feeling that they want me to get down and beg for my life or whatever. But I just walk, and it was 700 metres I have to walk there, and -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And where were they shooting? Was the shooting aimed at something?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: They were not -- I -- no hit and I didn't see any bullets on the street or something, but -- over my head, but I was a little bit scared because if you are drunk and shooting like that, you can also miss. So I was a little bit scared, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in -- on the third and fourth pages of your 1995 statement and, as well, at paragraphs 47 to 49 of your 2009 statement, you describe a foot patrol that you and your Sector Chief went on a little later that morning, and you describe how you were stopped at the same check-point that you had originally passed. You have marked that check-point with the letter K on the photograph attached to your statement, and you describe seeing military vehicles driven with soldiers leaving Knin, passing that check-point. And I'd like to ask you, approximately how many of these military vehicles did you see during this hour or so you were stopped at the check-point filled with goods?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Let's say -- I'm not sure, but at least ten of them. Ten vehicles were leaving at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you explained that the vehicles were loaded with goods, such as TVs, videos, and furniture.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: How was it that you were able to see these goods in the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: It was open, and -- on the back on the vehicles and it was open, so I could see -- I could see that it was goods going out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Were these vehicles trucks?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes. You can say truck, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at paragraph 48 of your 2008 statement, you state that at this time the check-point was manned by military police soldiers and civilian police. Do you remember approximately how many people manned this check-point at this time?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: On the first time when I came there at 7.00 in the morning, it was two or three military guys there, and when we came back it was also policija, so let's say six to eight people.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you've described in the third and fourth pages of your 1995 statement and paragraph 22 of your 2008 statement how after you passed the check-point you saw a lot of soldiers wearing the badge of the Puma Battalion carrying goods. What kind of goods did you see these soldiers carrying?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: It was -- most it was TV and video and, also, furniture.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you see what they were doing with the goods, where they were carrying them, what -- if they were putting them somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: They put it onto the trucks, and then they were driving outside of Knin somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And based on your observations, did the soldiers appear to be trying to hide what they were doing or were they acting more or less openly?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Openly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did the soldiers react in any way to the presence of you and your Sector Chief in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yeah. They ask us -- told us that it could be mines, so we shouldn't be there. We should not be at the place because it could be mines there, but we walked on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you see any activity that you could observe was aimed at trying to locate mines?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And can you give the Trial Chamber an idea as to how many soldiers you saw carrying goods in this way in Knin on the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Hard to say. If I say 50, it could be 100, it could be -- but at least 50 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at the fourth page of your 1995 statement, you describe that when you were at the policija station a man who claimed to be the chief of military police told you you were not allowed to be there and took you back to the UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did he gave you any reason why you were not allowed to be there?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: He said that no UN personnel were allowed to be outside, out in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did he tell you why?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And throughout the 6th of August, during your initial walk to the headquarters, the UN headquarters and during your later foot patrol, did you see any signs of any combat taking place in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the soldiers that you saw on the 6th of August, did it appear to that you they were on the alert for a possible combat or possible enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No. A lot of them were drunk, so I think they were celebrating.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at the fourth page of your 1995 statement, after you arrived back at the UN headquarters on the 6th, you describe how you observed soldiers taking cars which refugees had used to arrive at the UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Trial Chamber what you saw?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: At the HQ, I was standing at the gate and as soon as somebody coming to -- for protection inside the camp, they put the car, and after a while a soldier came, and they took the car and drive away.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And can you remember now approximately how many times you saw this happen, a car being driven by someone to take refuge and a soldier driving it away?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No, I can't say that, but we were talking about it inside, that it was not fair to steal like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And now I'd like to ask you a few questions about events in Knin after the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, if you would you not mind, I'd like to seek some clarification on one of the previous questions. That was your question about paragraph 48 of the 2008 statement. Mr. Widen, you answered a question as follows: "On the first time when I came there, 7.00 in the morning, it was two or three military guys there, and when we came back it was also policija, so let's say six to eight people." This answer suggests, at least in my understanding, that when you came there, there were two or three military guys and that when you returned that in addition to them, there was also policija. Now, if I look at your statement in paragraph 47, you further explain that the check-point was manned by HV soldiers. In paragraph 48, you explained that when you returned that it was then manned by military police soldiers and police. Now, it is not entirely clear to me what you saw when you returned. When you went, at least as what I understand from your statement and your testimony, is that these were soldiers. When you returned, it appears from your statement and from your testimony that there was policija; but were the soldiers replaced by military policemen, or were there military policemen in addition to - if I could call it that way - the plain soldiers that you had seen when you first passed this check-point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not the same people when I came back. It was other people there, and it was military police, military people and policija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you came, it was one category --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- soldiers. When you returned, it was soldiers, military police, and what you call policija? Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 33 of your 2008 statement, you describe seeing military vehicles loaded with goods going past the UN headquarters everyday. When you saw these vehicles go by, was there generally just one soldier there each vehicle, was there generally more than one soldier per vehicle, or was there no general pattern that you observed?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Normally, it was a driver and some people in the back, on -- on the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And was it a mixture of soldiers and civilians or just soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Soldiers. Only soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what kind of goods were these vehicles carrying?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: It was the same all the time, furniture and this electronic equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And are you able to estimate how many of these vehicles you saw in total going past the UN headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No, I can't. It -- but you can count them in -- it must be around 50 to 100 vehicles. It could be the same vehicles going and coming and reloading and coming back, I don't know, but it was many.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now I'd like if the witness could be shown Exhibit D65, and this is an UNCIVPOL report dated the 12th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's drafted by you, Mr. Widen, and it's discussed at paragraph 55 of your 2008 statement. It should be on the screen now in front of you. Do you -- are you able to see the document clearly?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you recall this incident?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: On the left side, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The left side is the -- is the English; the right side is a translation.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you can focus on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about this incident. When you and your UNCIVPOL colleague went into the house, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Inside, in the kitchen, on the chair, it was an older man sitting dead, and it had start smelling. And if I go inside the room there, it was a younger man lying just close to the -- to the window, and he was also dead. And it was warm that day, so perhaps -- I don't know how long they have been dead, but it smelled. So what we have to do in that time where we have to inform the policija about this. When we found any dead bodies, we have to inform the police about that, and they came to the spot, and then they told us we were lucky we didn't went inside because it was armed with the mines inside, and he also show us one mine in his hand. But we know that that wasn't true because we have been there before, but we didn't tell him about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When you say you didn't tell him about that, what didn't you tell him?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: We just say, Thank you, and then we left the spot there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, you say that the policeman said that you were lucky you didn't go inside.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you had been inside.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When the police arrived, were you still inside?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No. We were waiting outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what did -- what was your overall impression of this scene inside the house?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I don't know if I have the right English word, but execution. When you -- the man sitting on the chair, he was shoot -- shot where he was sitting, and I think the younger man were trying to escape and he was shot when he tried to escape.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you see any signs of bullet wounds?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No. This -- the bodies were -- let's say, when you have been dead for perhaps a couple of days in that warm weather, it was not that easy to -- we didn't touch them. We didn't try to know how -- how they got killed, but -- so this is something -- I can't say they were shot with one bullet or ten. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the report says that the bodies were taken to the hospital in Knin. Did you see the bodies being taken out of the house?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And were you ever able to confirm whether or not the bodies were taken to the Knin hospital?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you know why the report says that they were taken to the Knin hospital? Do you know where that information came from?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: If I remember right, the policija, when they came and took the bodies, they told us, We will take them to the -- I think it was from that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you remember if there was anyone else from the UN with you other than your UNCIVPOL colleague who is mentioned in this report when you went to this scene?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No, it was just --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, it was just the two of you? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. I'd just like to point out that the victims referenced in this report are Killing Victims number 162 and 163 as numbered in the clarification that the Prosecution filed on the 16th of July, and we've tendered the documents associated with these victims in our 5th of August motion to admit killing-related materials from the Bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Widen. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question to clarify one of your answers. You were asked whether these were trucks and then you said, You could call them trucks. What would you call trucks which are not trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but it's -- I know what -- in Swedish, we say "lastbil," but I don't know if anybody can speak -- but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact one of our legal officers who is not a trained interpreter, but if the parties would not object against Mr. Nilsson telling us in what he understands to be the English for what the witness just said. Mr. Nilsson, it's a truck? That's a truck. Could you give us -- could you give us an explanation as to a truck is a vehicle which is designed for carrying goods or personnel, more than just driver and one or two passengers. Now, could you give us an impression of the size of the -- of the part of the truck on which here, apparently, goods could be loaded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the front, you normally have a place for one or two -- two or three people sitting, the driver and someone else, and that's it. And then have you this long -- where you can put things on or put soldiers or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what was approximately the length of that part of the vehicle? Was it three metres, which we would call a very small truck, or would it be six or seven metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six or seven metres, yes. It was -- those -- not a small truck. It was medium, if I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have seen larger ones, but you have seen smaller ones as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were most of these trucks, what was the -- were they loaded heavily or slightly or ... could you give us an impression whether they were fully loaded or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fully loaded, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fully loaded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe, are you first to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Widen, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Widen.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Widen, I'd just like to ask you a couple of questions, several questions on matters that didn't come up in direct but were discussed in your two witness statements. And the first I'd like to address is, I notice in your 1995 statement - which, pardon me, is P721 - that you noted on paragraph 2 that you had initially come to Sector South and you were in another station in Benkovac but that you had to close that statement, and you note that: "During that time I was taken hostage for a few hours. On the 1st of May, I lost seven vehicles which were seized at gunpoint by Serb soldiers." Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And there was a degree of animosity between the Serbs and the UN during this period of time, was there not?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the -- what were the Serbs doing to the UN personnel? Why don't we start that way.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Normal people would have no problem with normal people, but you have kind of soldiers -- as I told you, I saw the same people in Knin later on. I saw these people in -- in Benkovac and -- this seems to have no in charge, if you understand what I say. They were doing whatever they liked to do, and they have a lot of arms, and I recognise one of the guy. He was like a Rambo, and he was the one who came into the station and took me as a hostage for a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did that include these Serbs stealing vehicles from the UN?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: They -- normally, at that time when he took hostage in the station he left with two of our trucks, and before that it was -- we got hijack on the roads. They stop us, one in the front on the way, and then we know that it's always one or two in the back, so if you try to back up and get away, we couldn't do that because they were shooting. So normally I just stopped the vehicle, went out, and give him the key. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When this was transpiring, Mr. Widen, did -- after it happened, did you complain to the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Of course, I went to the milicija station, and we always complained, but it seems to have no authority. We told the -- the milicija, yeah, there can you see one of our vehicles. Why can't you stop and give it back to us? But he couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And why couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Because there were military people who was in charge, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, was there a criminal element in this -- among these Serbs who were taking this -- these items?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I would say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me address you to an UNCIVPOL report. If I can pull up P218. Just for your reference, and it will come up on the screen, Mr. Widen, is a UNCIVPOL report. That was a report from 24 through 30 July 1995. If you just look at that front sheet, and if we could go into the fourth page. And if we could just blow up that Sector South item at the top. And -- can you see that okay, Mr. Widen?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I can read it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. In the area at the top of the page under Sector South, it notes that the Croat minority situation in this sector is seemingly worse than that of the Serb minority in Sector West. Do you remember Jan Elleby?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Mr. Elleby testified before this Court on May the 23rd, 2008, and at page 3469 he was asked this question after being read this same passage, and I can just start it from line 20: "Now, if you can just take that top paragraph, Sector South there, it notes that in Sector South the Croat minority situation in the sector is seemingly worse than that of the Serb minority in south west. Now, Mr. Elleby, had this pattern abuse of the Croat minorities gone on for some time as you understood the situation in Sector South?" Answer: "Yes, you could say that. And also, there were a lot of restrictions of movement, so from time to time we couldn't move into certain areas as this paper shows. In the end of July, we couldn't actually move anywhere." Now, was that your experience, sir, that the -- prior to Operation Storm that the remaining Croatian population had a very difficult time in Sector South at the hands of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Perhaps they had. We were helping them with food and visit them, and -- but -- yeah, they have a hard time there, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And were they getting a hard time at the -- from the Serbs who had -- who were in charge of the area?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's move ahead just a bit. I'll move -- staying on this item on the screen, if we can just look to the first page. If we can go back two pages, please. It's actually not the first -- one more page up, I'm sorry. And if we go down to that area, notes on Sector South. You see that on the bottom there, Mr. Widen?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we note -- let me just get the last couple of sentences: "All CIVPOL patrols in the area have been suspended by the Sector Chief. UNCIVPOL stations at Knin, Korenica are being kept open with just two monitors and one interpreter. Monitors have been advised to stay in their private accommodations to minimise the risk of hostage-taking." Staying with this exhibit, and let me just note a couple of items for you. If we can move up on that same item, three more pages, and again in that Sector South in -- in, yeah, paragraph 7. That's correct. Without reading it, if we can just look at that paragraph under Sector South, it discusses the murder of a Kenyan battalion soldier and the robbery of 80 litres of fuel that was witnessed by CIVPOL. Now, this -- is this consistent with what you said before of this criminal element within the Serb military?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I can't recognise anything of this. I haven't -- I haven't seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you can take look at it, sir. This is a UNCIVPOL report.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: From who?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: From UNCIVPOL headquarters, and it's the weekly report, 24-30 July, 1995, where they chronicle each particular sector, and the inclusion that we just had concerning the Kenyan battalion soldier that had been murdered and the robbery of 80 litres of fuel is in the area that is under Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm. But about this murder, I didn't know that. I haven't heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, sir, let me then -- let me go back to your statement itself and talk about some other items and specifically in your 1995 statement, if I may. Could you look at the -- and you can look at this. It's on your 1995 statement, which is 721, paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you have the hard copy before you, Mr. Widen, but we can wait for the screen if that's easier for you. It's on page 4 of that document, sir. That's also on the screen if it is easier for you.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we talked a little bit -- you talked a bit about this criminal element among the Serbs that was in existence prior to Operation Storm. I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 7 at the -- we can just read this. "Prior to 4 August, there a lot of people living in Knin, and according to our interpreters it was impossible to find a flat. Schools were functioning at all levels. We had a civil police station beside a big school where there were a large numbers of children until they broke up for summer holidays. The two markets were open for business. There was a particularly large range of products, but most of the shops were open. No banks were open, but a black' --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, did you misspeak? I also heard what we find on the transcript that there was a -- whereas the text you're reading that it is it that there wasn't a particularly large range of products.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I misspoke. There wasn't. There wasn't a particularly large range of products, but most of the shops were open. "No banks were open, but a black market was operating for money."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what this black market was, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I -- I can't remember, but it probably was that if you like to have local money you have to change it with the civilian. I can't remember this, not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, was there a black market for stolen goods in the Krajina when you were there that the Serbs were buying and selling?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There was not?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No. What I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That you know. Well, let me turn our attention back to P218, if I may, the fourth page in on 218. And if I could go to the quality of life of section, if we could just blow that up, number 6 at the bottom. And in the middle of that paragraph, if I may, it notes that the "forced closure of businesses not to mention the critical cut-off of the Livno valley supply route is bound to have adverse socio-economic affects. The road through the Bosanski Grahovo was the main smuggling pipeline to Knin, the alternative through Donji Lapac being more long-winded." Now, the main -- this main smuggling pipeline that this report is referring to, Mr. Widen, do you know what was being smuggled through this pipeline through Bosanski Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I haven't seen -- this is it not what I have been written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. It is -- this is just a UNCIVPOL report --

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yeah. But I haven't seen, and I didn't know that it was smuggled. No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware of organised crime elements in the Krajina prior to Operation Storm dealing in the black market and smuggling throughout Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just going to shift gears and move to another topic, Mr. Widen, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you put a question to the witness, and just for me to better understand the question, you suggested although the witness didn't know anything about it that there was a smuggling pipeline, and what kind of things I have to -- I mean, what -- was it an open question, could smuggling be anything, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think -- I think it was virtually -- fuel. I think it was arms. It was a variety of different things. I don't want to testify here, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I do understand. But apparently you had an idea of what you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- talking, the witness's comments, about, and I just wanted to know what was on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And also in my mind was also furnishings, electronic goods. All of those things were smuggled back and forth at escalated prices with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you included both matters on which the witness has not testified in whatever way and including, also, matters on which the witness testified as goods being transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Judge, the first matter on the black market for money was in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But, of course, you then asked whether -- what he meant by that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether it was goods, stolen goods or not. I -- of course, it came to my mind that even money can be stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that apparently was not what you were asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I am asking for any type of black market operations in any fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to this, this is a UNCIVPOL report talking about a smuggling pipeline, and Your Honour, you have been a lawyer, as well as I do, long enough that smuggling has a certain negative connotation that indicates that it's not legal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- or it has something torrid, so that was why I was -- yes, this wasn't in his statement. That's why I'd given this in a UNCIVPOL report and he was from Sector South during this period of time given as explored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness said he knew about the money, the black market -- the money, black market, and he said he didn't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I just wanted to know whether your questions were limited or whether they had a wider range, and they apparently have a wide -- a broad scope, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They have a wider range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the -- just for clarification, Your Honour, the witness's knowledge is obviously limited in this regard, and I'm going move off this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. No, it was just for my understanding of what the question was specifically about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I may, just several matters, and I would like to touch on a couple of your statements that you had -- in your 1995 statement in paragraph 8, if you can go to that, sir. That's page 4, paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted that the soldiers seemed very ill-disciplined, and there were a lot of shooting at night, and there was regiment in Knin and there seemed -- they seemed to be better disciplined, but in town the soldiers were often drunk. Tell us a little about this regiment in Knin that was more disciplined.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I don't know anything. I said -- the guys I saw at this school yard, and the others were sitting in the cafes were more like they have some -- what they call the Black Tigers, I think, and it was more like people from that -- I don't know. It was -- they were not disciplined, anyway, those who were sitting in a cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the ones that were in the school, and I think that you designated this area as -- in your chart, if I may, if we can go to your chart. You put a letter around the area where that school was.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what number -- what letter was that?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Let's see now ... it's hard to remember now how ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can clarify it later, Mr. Widen, but this school where these soldiers were, these are the 500 soldiers you were talking about when the Chamber was asking you about it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this was right next to the civilian police station?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And they came to that location after school let out, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes, when the children left for summer vacation, so the soldier took over the school, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And without giving us an exact date, do you recall when they came to that school?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But these are the soldiers that you found to be more disciplined?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever learn that they were JNA -- or the Yugoslav troops from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever learn anything about where these troops came from?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What indicated to you that they were more disciplined than the other troops in town?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Let's say they have different uniforms, and it seems that they have some people in charge, and -- just the feeling I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted in your testimony at -- this is page 31 at line 4 that they were called the Black Tigers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I think it was the Black Tigers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you recall what their uniform looked like?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say "Black Tigers," are you referring to Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I think -- because -- I think Arkans have a camp outside Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you're on your feet, but I don't hear you, so I do not know how to interpret the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was just waiting for a moment. I'm sorry to interrupt. I just was wondering if the question was suggesting that the Black Tigers were the same unit that the witness was referring to as the 500 stationed at the school, and that's not how I interpreted his earlier answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but as I earlier said, a debate on the interpretation of the statement of the witness is not -- if there is any misrepresentation of the statement of the witness, then perhaps without explaining in the presence of the witness what you are talking about, refer, perhaps, the Chamber to any matter where you say this misrepresent because it's inconsistent with what we find we find on page so-and-so, line so-and-so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. I do think it might be a misrepresentation, maybe unintentional or maybe it's my misunderstanding. It thought that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Page 32, line 13 and 14, was a question referring back -- I think there's a mistake, I think it's page 31, that this unit was called the Black Tigers. If you go back to page 31, line 4, I believe the Black Tigers was not referring to this regiment at the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, and again, if you want to explain clearly why it is it misrepresented, do it in such a way that the witness is not put on notice on what you consider is the right representation, but just draw the attention of the Chamber to pages, paragraphs, or lines, and then we'll read them and then we'll see whether there's any ground for the objection. Page 3, line 4, you're talking about the first statement, the 1995 statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It was all in the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Line 31. It was page -- page 31 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. But then if you go back to page 3, in line 4 -- page 3, line 4 stands for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It should be page 31.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Page 31, line 4, of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's page 31, line -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can easily clarify and just ask the question. It may be easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- yes. If it's clearer to you than it is to me, Mr. Kehoe, please, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can just ask the question again and, you know, to the extent there's any ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned there were 500 soldiers, the well-disciplined soldiers at the school. Were those the soldiers that you believed were named the Tigers?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Those are -- there's a different group. Now, what were the soldiers at the school known as, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I don't know, but they were not the Tigers because the Tigers, they were working, let's say, for themselves. So these people in the school yard were, I would say, normal soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the element that you described as the Tigers, where were they?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I don't know if those who were sitting in the cafe I said and were drinking a lot, if those guys belonged to the Tigers, I don't know. I don't know. But -- no, I don't know that. But the Tigers have a camp outside of Benkovac, that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, for one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this element that -- this element of the Tigers that was outside of Benkovac, was that Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: So I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony at page 6 at line 17, you said that you saw Mladic in Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And tell us about you seeing Mladic in -- General Mladic in Knin.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: It was at the school yard, and he was standing in the middle of his soldiers there, and I recognise him because of the special hat, and we were talking about him at the HQ, so I saw him there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you say the school yard, this is the same location where these well-disciplined troops were?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And approximately when was this?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Didn't I write that? I think I have been writing down that I saw Mladic somewhere. I think so. So that should be -- but I can't say. It should be in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be towards the end of July, approximately, say, the 30th of July?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time -- let me read you something, again, from Mr. Elleby, and this is it at page 3474, line 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not exactly sure where this is going, but if it's similar to the previous question that was asked where this witness was read portions of someone's else's evidence on the matter, I thought that there was an understanding that before that stuff was taken that the witness could simply be asked about the matter, and then if it was necessary for whatever reason, the other witnesses's statements or evidence could be put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I think that was the guidance. Of course, I do not know what you're going to ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but if it was what Ms. Gustafson was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That has not -- that has not been the practice, and certainly, that has not been a practice that's been followed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think, as a matter of fact, that when there was -- when there were objections that not first put to the witness what other witnesses have testified but, rather, first ask the witness about the event and then if there's any need to tell the witness that someone else has testified in a similar way or in a different way; that's at least the guidance for this moment if that was on your mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, towards the end of July, a few days in July and up to the end of July, did you observe more and more military vehicles and more and more uniformed personnel in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and, also, I saw some people I know from Benkovac, milicija guy, the chief of the milicija in Benkovac at that time, and he was dressed in uniform now, so some kind of mobilisation, I would say it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And likewise, you noted in your 1995 statement P721 on paragraph 8, and you can take a look at that, sir, you note in paragraph 8 that during July, when you moved to Knin, there were many Serb soldiers and a lot of military convoys also passed through town. The next sentence says, "For the most part the soldiers sat in the cafes always carrying their weapons."

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next sentence: "I saw a number of tanks passing through Knin a few days before the assault." Do you know where these tanks went to a few days before the assault, and I assume you're talking about Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I would say they were going through Knin and -- I can't say where they were going, but they just passed Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, going down a couple of other sentences in the same paragraph, you note: "On some of the Nissan pickup trucks which were stolen from the UN, heavy machine-guns or rocket launchers had been mounted."

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know what type of rocket launchers these were?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No, but I can see a different machine-gun, and when you have these like missiles, missiles --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Missiles, yes.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Missiles. A small one of those, I would say it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And they were on the back of trucks?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you observe them driving around?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know where they were going?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how many of these trucks with -- with rocket launchers on the back did you see?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how about trucks with heavy machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I would say all the trucks that had been stolen from UN have -- have a machine gun on the back, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how many approximately are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I got lost around seven in Benkovac, so I can't just answer for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were UN vehicles in other areas of Sector South taken from UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did they likewise have either machine-guns or rocket launchers on the back?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I can't say. I saw it in Benkovac, and I saw it in Knin, but -- I went, also, to Obrovac, but, no, I can't remember if I saw any there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall the fall of Grahovo when the HV defeated the ARSK and Bosanski Grahovo fell in late July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Can you take that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the city of -- or the town of Bosanski Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is up north, I guess, north-east of Knin and had been taken by the HV on approximately 28 July 1995. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, would you agree, sir, that towards the latter part of July in Knin people started to get very upset about HV victories against the ARSK. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us talk a little bit about people leaving Knin, and I know you talked a little bit about that with the Prosecution. If I could -- if I may, ask you to take a look at -- well, sir, prior to -- the night prior to Operation Storm, did you know anything about people leaving Knin in an organised fashion?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I can't say what happened during -- it started there at 5.00 in the morning, and I was inside my house all the time until I went to this guy Boris so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the night prior to that, prior to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know of the Serbs leaving in an organised fashion?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Organised, I don't know, but some were leaving, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me read you -- if I could bring Exhibit 514, page 2. This is an interview given by then-Major Claude Bellerose of -- he's a Canadian major stationed in UN Sector South, and if I could go to -- excuse me, did I say -- D514. I apologise. D514. Now if we could go to the second page, the left-hand column towards the top. On the third line down, the question going to Major Bellerose: "When did the bombardment of the city itself begin?" Mr. Bellerose notes: "I believe it was 5.00 in the morning on the 4th of August." Question: "Then they began to shell Knin immediately?" "Yes." "But -- okay. But then the flood of refugees continued into Knin, correct?" "Well, on the refugee side a lot of people from Knin fled that -- that night just before the bombardment, just like someone had given them a heads up and they fled. It was apparently well organised." Are you familiar with that, sir, of people leaving?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No, no. I mean, perhaps he was on the streets so he can see it, but I was inside, so I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in your 1995 statement, and I just want to take us forward, you noted in paragraph 3 -- this is on the second page of paragraph 3: "During Friday night, I could hear the noise of many vehicles. The neighbour on the block above left his car. There were three occupants in it as well as loads of luggage, so I gathered they were fleeing." You clarified, oh, you said something further, that you're -- in P722 at paragraph 50, and that's your 19 -- or excuse me, 2008 statement, where you clarify that, and you noted: "As far as I could tell, most civilians, around 80 per cent, left during Friday night and during the day on Saturday." Now, did you observe that, sir, or did you just hear it?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I just hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the heaviest shelling was in fact in the early morning hours of the 4th, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes, and also the same in the morning of the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you heard these individuals leaving on the -- beginning on the evening of the 4th, the Friday night?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: The shelling started at 5.00 on the 4th, and this evening there were -- I heard the noise about people leaving, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you D137, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could just cover this one document before the break, Your Honour. I think we're almost at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Widen, this is an order by President Milan Martic of the Republic of Serb Krajina from 4 August 1995 at 16.45 hours, 4.45 in the afternoon, ordering the evacuation of the municipalities of Benkovac, Obrovac, Knin, Drnis, and Gracac. Now, this is in the afternoon of the 4th, and this before you heard people evacuating, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: It was later on the 4th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were discussing these matters with the Prosecution and you came to your opinion where you were made aware of the fact that an evacuation order had been issued by the president of the Republic of Serb Krajina --

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- in the afternoon of the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: I haven't seen this before, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you know nothing about this?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Widen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this is the usual time for a break. Could we get any indication as far as timing is concerned, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should move through this in an hour, I think. I really -- a lot of -- if I may, Judge, just by clarification a lot of -- if the witness says "I don't know" about something, that certainly will cut things down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I do understand that that would shorten the cross-examination. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, zero to half an hour, depending on what happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll have a break, and we'll resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Widen, I'd like to direct your attention to the portion of your statements that talks about the actual shelling of Knin, and if we could turn our attention back to your 1995 statement, P721, at paragraph 6. I believe it's in the just prior pages, at the bottom of 6. And you note that -- at paragraph 6: "My assessment after having walked around Knin is that most shells had landed in the residential areas. As far as could I see, no public buildings had been hit." And you gave us -- and by the way, Mr. Widen, how many times did you actually travel around the city of Knin after Operation Storm to make these observations?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Five or six times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you also noted that you didn't go to the eastern part of town. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But let us just look at the -- you gave us a map that is before you that has the areas that have been designated as being hit by shellfire, and I took the liberty of putting them on a different map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can bring up 1D43-0001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, these are the areas, all of the areas that you circled in your map that was introduced by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if you would not mind that I intervene for a second. I'm quite happy that you provide us with this map. I hope that the Prosecution agrees with the way in which you've translated the data on the other map because, Ms. Gustafson, if have you maps which in print appear to be purple, red is, I must admit, together with blue the worst colour you could use to do the markings. It's almost impossible for us to verify exactly where the markings are, so -- and this is not the first time that we find those red markings on maps of the same colour. So if for the future the Prosecution would keep in mind that any new map being marked, either the basic colour of the map to be different or the markings to be in a different, while contrasting, colour because I have even difficulties to verify whether what you have put on your map is what we have on our maps. Now, I take it, and I would be very happy if you could you confirm the accuracy of what Mr. Kehoe presented to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm seeing it for the first time now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps take your time, and apparently -- you must be in a position to confirm it because you present the map, so apparently you are able to see where the circles are, and I verified with the other judges. We apparently all three are of an age that it becomes too difficult to -- to look at this, and I apologise for my colleague to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, you don't have to apologise. I'm that age too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I do not apologise -- Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, and we expect a confirmation by the Prosecution and, again, it's an appreciated that you give it to us now in a more legible form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Widen, do you understand what I tried to do? I tried to transpose it on a map. Okay. If we could go to the next map. These locations I have designated are the areas in your witness statement where you have stated to the Prosecution that you observed shell damage, and I have taken out areas that -- where you didn't say there was any shell damage such as in the cemetery, which is L, and other areas where there -- you did not discuss the shell damage. Okay, sir, are you with me?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And the area of red will become significant for you in a moment. I do want to say to you, by way of clarification, in your designation of where you lived in your 1995 statement, you noted that you lived on L. Marunda 32 in Knin. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ERIK LENNART WIDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
